title: Rafel Cirer-Sastre
text:
Associate Professor of Kinesiology · INEFC Lleida, Universitat de Lleida


Many measurements strike me as more convincing than reliable.

PhD opportunity Research Publications
That is the thread through everything I work on: how we measure what exercise does to the body, and what we can claim from what we have measured. Since 2022 I have also coordinated research support at the centre.
Applied biostatistics runs through all three: time-course modelling, Bayesian regression, systematic review and meta-analysis. More about the research →

title: Rafel Cirer-Sastre
text:
The question behind EXCURSE



A joint angle does not tell you at what length a muscle worked. EXCURSE compares four muscle excursion ranges, each defined against the limits of voluntary shortening and lengthening.


I lead EXCURSE (2025–2028), funded by INEFC under reference 2025 PINEF 00018 and co-led with Xavier Peirau Terès.

title: PhD opportunity: EXCURSE
text:
I do not expect you to arrive knowing how to do a PhD. A PhD is, precisely, the time we will spend learning how.
I have room for two or three doctoral candidates within EXCURSE — Muscle Excursion Range in Strength Training: Implications for Performance and Injury Prevention (2025–2028).
The rest of this page explains each of those points, and how I supervise.

title: PhD opportunity: EXCURSE
text:
Funding and conditions
This is not a funded predoctoral position. EXCURSE has funding for research costs, but no predoctoral contract has been awarded. You would need to apply for and win a competitive predoctoral scholarship, such as AGAUR/FI, FPU, or an equivalent scheme in your own country. I can help develop the application, but I cannot guarantee its outcome. Supervisory capacity for two or three candidates does not imply that scholarships will be awarded.
The work is on-site at the faculty in Lleida, not remote. It has associated teaching duties.
Admission requires an official master’s degree, in accordance with the requirements of the UdL doctoral programme in Physical Activity and Sports.

title: PhD opportunity: EXCURSE
text:
The research
EXCURSE examines how the muscle lengths used during strength training shape subsequent adaptation. We compare training across different regions of muscle excursion and study changes in muscle architecture, strength, neuromuscular activation, and mechanical properties.
A doctoral project could address how adaptations differ across regions of muscle excursion, how responses vary between people, or how those responses develop over time. I may also consider proposals on field-test validation or the modelling of physiological responses to exercise when there is a clear question and a strong methodological fit.

title: PhD opportunity: EXCURSE
text:
How we will work
We will meet every week. The purpose is not to account for what you have done, but to create a regular space to think aloud, revisit decisions, and agree on the next step.
You will have freedom to plan your work and explore your own ideas. I will ask questions, help identify problems, and offer guidance while you develop your own judgement. I will not write the papers or solve the analyses for you, but I will not assume that you already know how to do them.
The aim is that, by the end, you can formulate a question, design a study, analyse the data, write the work, and defend your decisions without depending on me.

title: PhD opportunity: EXCURSE
text:
How we do research
The work sits at the intersection of exercise physiology, measurement, and modelling. We will read, write, code, and prepare publications almost entirely in English. Meetings may be in Catalan or Spanish.
We currently use R for data analysis because it is the most useful tool for our work, not because it is an identity or a doctrine. Tools may change when another option genuinely improves the work.
Artificial intelligence will be part of the workflow for coding, exploring ideas, and reviewing writing. It will not replace judgement. We will distinguish between what can be delegated, what must be checked, and what cannot be accepted without understanding it.

title: PhD opportunity: EXCURSE
text:
What I look for
You do not need prior publications or advanced statistical training. You do need curiosity, consistency, and a willingness to develop independence.
I am looking for someone willing to write from the beginning, work with data before feeling fully confident, and ask why an analysis works or fails rather than only whether it produces a statistically significant result. I value the ability to learn more than prior skills.

title: PhD opportunity: EXCURSE

How to begin
Talk to me before starting any formal application. Write briefly about your academic background, the questions that interest you, and the scholarship scheme for which you may be eligible.

title: Research
text: The question that ties my research together is how we measure what exercise does to the body and what we can claim from what we have measured. Three research lines follow from it. They do not carry the same weight or belong to the same stage of my career.

title: Research
text:
Strength training and muscle mechanics
This is the active line I am building: how the body adapts to strength training, and whether describing exercise from the perspective of the muscle explains those adaptations better than joint motion alone.
I lead EXCURSE — Muscle Excursion Range in Strength Training: Implications for Performance and Injury Prevention (2025–2028), funded by INEFC under reference 2025 PINEF 00018 and co-led with Xavier Peirau Terès. We compare training across different regions of muscle excursion and study changes in muscle architecture, strength, neuromuscular activation, and mechanical properties.
The open questions are whether adaptations differ according to the region of muscle excursion used during training, and how much responses vary between people and over time.
The antecedent of this line is a meta-analysis of contralateral effects after unilateral strength training. More recent related work includes conventional resistance training compared with core exercise in road cyclists and pedalling muscle stiffness across cyclist performance levels.
I am recruiting doctoral researchers for this line. Read about the PhD opportunity.

title: Research
text:
Field-test validation and endurance performance
This is my most applied line: how we measure endurance performance outside the laboratory, and where a practical field test stops being an adequate substitute for a laboratory protocol.
My work has examined functional threshold power, prediction of VO2max from a short maximal test, and the variability of time to exhaustion at an estimated threshold. Studies include comparisons of functional threshold power with lactate thresholds, a five-minute power-based test to predict VO2max, and time to exhaustion at estimated functional threshold power.
The open questions are which field-test estimates remain valid at the level of the individual athlete, and how test error, performance level, and between-person variability should affect interpretation.
Main collaborators: Sebastian Sitko and Isaac López-Laval (Universidad de Zaragoza).

title: Research
text:
Cardiac biomarkers after exercise
This is my most established line, although it is now less central to my work: how the body responds acutely to exercise, particularly how cardiac troponin changes in children and adolescents.
I have focused on the time course of the response rather than a single post-exercise value. The work includes a systematic review and meta-analysis in healthy children and adolescents, a study of maturational status and cardiac troponin T in young swimmers, and a comparison of modelled cTnT and cTnI kinetics.
The open questions are how sampling time changes the interpretation of an observed value, and how maturation, exercise load, and between-person variability shape the response.
Main collaborators: Keith George (Liverpool John Moores University), Alejandro Legaz-Arrese (Universidad de Zaragoza), and Luis Enrique Carranza-García (Universidad Autónoma de Nuevo León).

title: Research
text:
The method underneath
Applied biostatistics is not a fourth research line. It is the perspective from which I approach the other three.
I work with mixed-effects models, Bayesian regression, systematic reviews, and meta-analysis. For repeated biological measurements, I model observations within individuals and the shape of change over time rather than analyse each time point as if it were independent. I also conduct statistical analysis for the Clinical Neurosciences group at IRBLleida, including the REMOTE-CAT stroke trial.
Statistics begins before the data arrive: it helps formulate the question, design the study, and establish what the study will be able to support.
